**Visual analysis:**

- **Affected part:** Wheat leaf (long, narrow blade — typical cereal/wheat)
- **Color pattern:** Predominantly green leaf with scattered white/pale patches and short elongated streaks distributed across the blade surface
- **Texture:** The white areas appear superficial and somewhat powdery/fluffy in character — not sunken lesions, not vascular stripes, not necrotic blotches
- **Distribution:** Irregular but widespread across the leaf surface; patches vary from small discrete colonies to slightly elongated areas

**Reasoning through candidates:**

| Disease | Expected signs | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| **Powdery Mildew** | White powdery colonies/patches on leaf surface, superficial mycelial growth | ✅ Strong match |
| Stripe Rust | Yellow-orange urediniospore stripes parallel to veins | ✗ No orange/yellow |
| Septoria Leaf Blotch | Tan-brown blotches with pycnidia dots | ✗ No brown necrosis |
| Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus | Mosaic chlorosis, streak mottling | ✗ Not mosaic |
| Cephalosporium Stripe | White-yellow full-length vein-bound stripes | ✗ Not full-length stripes |
| Bacterial Streak | Water-soaked brown linear lesions | ✗ No brown streaks |

The white, superficial, powdery-looking patches scattered across the green leaf surface are the classic hallmark of **Powdery Mildew** (*Blumeria graminis* f. sp. *tritici*) — the white colonies are fungal mycelium and conidia growing epiphytically on the leaf surface.

This distribution and appearance is characteristic of Blumeria graminis powdery mildew colonies — epiphytic white mycelial growth on the leaf surface. No orange/yellow uredinia (ruling out rusts), no brown necrosis (ruling out Septoria/Tan Spot), and no mosaic chlorosis (ruling out viral diseases)."}
